solution.concept_anchor: CBI non-statutory status and 1963 Resolution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students routinely assume that a body as powerful and prominent as the CBI must have been created by an Act of Parliament, making the 'CBI Act' option feel authoritative.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option suggesting CBI was created by a dedicated Act of Parliament — no such 'CBI Act' exists.
Eliminate options linking CBI's name to a court judgment or presidential order — it was conferred by a Home Ministry Resolution.
Confirm that the DSPE Act 1946 is the operative statute and the name 'CBI' originates from a 1963 executive resolution.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here exploits the assumption that an agency as prominent as the CBI must have explicit statutory backing of its own. Students familiar with bodies like the CVC or NIA — which have dedicated Acts — unconsciously extend this logic to the CBI. The option naming a 'CBI Act' sounds authoritative precisely because such an act should exist but does not. Only a student who knows that 'CBI' is a name conferred by a Home Ministry Resolution of 1963, while the operational basis remains the DSPE Act of 1946, will answer correctly.
solution.final_explanation:
The CBI's legal architecture is frequently misunderstood. It operates under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 — a pre-independence legislation originally enacted for wartime procurement corruption. There is no dedicated 'CBI Act.'

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No statute called the 'Central Bureau of Investigation Act' exists in Indian law.
• Option (b) — Correct: The name 'CBI' was conferred by a Home Ministry Resolution dated 1 April 1963; the agency's operational powers derive from the DSPE Act, 1946.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Lokpal Act 2013 references CBI in certain provisions but did not create or name it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 governs offences investigated by the CBI but is not its constitutive instrument.

Value Addition:
• Because CBI lacks its own statute, it is not a statutory body in the strict sense — unlike the CVC or NIA.
• The non-statutory character means CBI has no suo motu powers of investigation in states.
• Demands for a dedicated 'CBI Act' have been repeatedly raised by the Second ARC and Parliamentary Standing Committees.

solution.concept_anchor: DSPE Act 1946 — Section 3 and Section 5 scope

statement_analysis.statement: The DSPE Act, 1946 was originally enacted to investigate offences of bribery and corruption arising from wartime procurement during British India.
statement_analysis.reason: The DSPE was created specifically to address procurement-related corruption during World War II, making this historically accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 3 of the DSPE Act, the Central Government can extend CBI's jurisdiction to any offence it deems fit without any notification requirement.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 3 requires the Central Government to formally notify specific offences — CBI's subject-matter jurisdiction is not a blanket power but depends on a specific executive notification.

statement_analysis.statement: Section 5 of the DSPE Act provides the basis for extending CBI's powers and jurisdiction to Union Territories beyond Delhi.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 5 enables extension of the DSPE's territorial reach to Union Territories, forming the constitutional basis of CBI's jurisdiction outside Delhi.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it includes Statement 2 which sounds procedurally accurate to students who know Section 3 exists but do not know the notification requirement is mandatory, not discretionary.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is historically accurate — DSPE was a wartime anti-corruption measure; retain it.
Statement 2 adds 'without any notification requirement' — this scope-extension makes it false; Section 3 mandates notification. Eliminate options including Statement 2.
Statement 3 correctly identifies Section 5 as the Union Territory extension provision; retain it.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is crafted to exploit partial knowledge. Students who know that Section 3 empowers the Central Government to extend CBI jurisdiction often miss the critical qualifier: this must be done through a specific notification. The addition of 'without any notification requirement' transforms a true fact into a false one — a classic scope-extension trap. A student who only remembers the power exists but not its procedural constraint will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The DSPE Act, 1946 is the foundational statute underpinning all CBI operations. Understanding its key sections is essential for prelims.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The DSPE was established during World War II to address rampant corruption in government procurement for the war effort. It is one of few pre-independence statutes still in active use.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Section 3 does empower the Central Government to extend CBI's jurisdiction, but this extension must be done through a formal notification specifying the offences. A blanket, notification-free power does not exist — CBI cannot automatically investigate all central government matters.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 5 explicitly provides for the extension of DSPE powers to Union Territories, which is the legal basis for CBI conducting investigations in UTs beyond Delhi.

Value Addition:
• Entry 80 of the Union List (List I) provides the constitutional basis for Parliament legislating on the DSPE/CBI as a central investigative force.
• Post-independence, the DSPE Act was retained under Article 372, which continued pre-constitutional laws.
• The notification mechanism under Section 3 means Parliament — not just the executive — can influence CBI's functional remit.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI jurisdiction — three case categories and suo motu limits

statement_analysis.statement: Regular Cases (RC) handled by CBI pertain to corruption involving central government employees under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
statement_analysis.reason: RC cases are precisely defined as corruption cases against central government employees under the PC Act — this statement is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Preliminary Enquiries (PE) may be initiated by CBI based on its own intelligence, referrals from ministries, or court orders.
statement_analysis.reason: PEs cover cases referred by ministries, courts, or arising from CBI's own intelligence — all three sources are valid, making this statement correct.

statement_analysis.statement: CBI can suo motu register cases involving serious crimes affecting national interest in any state, without requiring prior state consent.
statement_analysis.reason: CBI has no suo motu power to register FIRs in states without their consent under Section 6 of the DSPE Act — this is a core constitutional limitation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students aware that CBI handles high-profile national crimes may assume it must have suo motu powers for 'national interest' cases, making Statement 3 feel correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 accurately describes RC cases — corruption + PC Act + central employees. This is correct, so eliminate options that mark it incorrect.
Statement 2 correctly identifies all three PE initiation sources. This is correct.
Statement 3 claims suo motu power in any state — this directly contradicts Section 6 of DSPE Act. This is NOT correct.
Only Statement 3 is incorrect — the question asks which is NOT correct, so select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the widespread misconception that a national-level agency like the CBI must have plenary suo motu powers. The phrase 'national interest' makes the claim feel constitutionally justified. However, CBI's jurisdiction in states is strictly subject to state consent under Section 6. Students who conflate CBI with NIA (which does have suo motu powers) are particularly vulnerable to this trap.
solution.final_explanation:
CBI's operational jurisdiction is divided into three functional categories, each with distinct initiation mechanisms.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Regular Cases (RCs) are the bread-and-butter of CBI's anti-corruption work — corruption cases against central government employees tried under the PC Act, 1988.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Preliminary Enquiries (PEs) are initial-stage investigations that may be triggered by ministry referrals, court directions, or CBI's own field intelligence — all three pathways are valid.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This is the NOT correct statement. CBI has no inherent suo motu power to investigate state-subject crimes without state consent. Section 6 of the DSPE Act is an absolute requirement. The only exceptions are court-ordered investigations under Articles 226/142 or cases involving central employees on central premises.

Value Addition:
• The third category — Special Crimes — covers terrorism, organised crime, and bank fraud referred by the Centre or courts, but still requires either notification or judicial direction in state territory.
• NIA, by contrast, has explicit suo motu powers under the NIA Act, 2008 — a critical distinction tested frequently.
• The consent requirement is rooted in 'Police' being Entry 2, List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 6 DSPE Act — consent types and withdrawal

statement_analysis.statement: Section 6 of the DSPE Act requires CBI to obtain the consent of the State Government before conducting investigations within that state.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 6 unambiguously mandates state consent as a prerequisite for CBI operations within state territory.

statement_analysis.statement: General consent given by a state to CBI is irrevocable and cannot be withdrawn once granted.
statement_analysis.reason: Several states including West Bengal, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Kerala have withdrawn their general consent, demonstrating it is not irrevocable.

statement_analysis.statement: After a state withdraws general consent, CBI must obtain fresh case-specific consent for each new investigation in that state.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-withdrawal, the blanket permission lapses and CBI must seek specific consent for every individual case — or obtain a court order.

statement_analysis.statement: A Supreme Court or High Court direction to investigate can override the Section 6 consent requirement, allowing CBI to operate in a non-consenting state.
statement_analysis.reason: Judicial directions under Articles 142 and 226 constitute a recognized override of the Section 6 consent requirement, as affirmed in multiple Supreme Court judgments.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students aware of court override powers and the withdrawal issue may incorrectly count Statement 2 as correct, believing general consent once given has some permanent legal effect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is the foundational rule — Section 6 consent is mandatory. Mark correct.
Statement 2 claims irrevocability — multiple states have withdrawn consent, disproving this. Mark incorrect.
Statement 3 accurately describes the case-specific consent requirement post-withdrawal. Mark correct.
Statement 4 correctly identifies judicial override as an established mechanism. Mark correct.
Three of four are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial-truth trap. Students who know that general consent is a recognized legal mechanism and that it simplifies CBI operations may assume it carries some permanence — especially since withdrawing it is a politically charged act. The statement sounds like a reasonable legal principle ('once granted, cannot be revoked') but is factually wrong. States' withdrawal of general consent has been a significant constitutional development, particularly in the context of Centre–State relations.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 6 of the DSPE Act is the pivot of CBI's federal jurisdiction. Understanding both types of consent and their implications is critical.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 6 is an absolute requirement. CBI cannot bypass it unilaterally in state territory.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: General consent is revocable. States like West Bengal, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Kerala have formally withdrawn it, forcing CBI to seek case-specific permission each time.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Post-withdrawal, the blanket permission ceases. Each new investigation requires a fresh specific consent or a court order.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Courts acting under Articles 142 and 226 can direct CBI investigations regardless of state consent — a judicial override rooted in constitutional supremacy.

Value Addition:
• The consent mechanism reflects the constitutional design of 'Police' as a State List subject (Entry 2, List II).
• Withdrawal of general consent does not affect cases already registered before withdrawal.
• The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010) held that High Courts can direct CBI investigations even in states that have withdrawn consent.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI vs NIA suo motu powers and legal basis
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places NIA with suo motu powers but incorrectly assigns CBI's Union Territory jurisdiction as a general suo motu power, which partially-prepared students accept without scrutiny.
elimination_logic: CBI's suo motu power is limited to Union Territories and cases involving central employees on central premises — match A with 2.
NIA Act 2008 explicitly grants suo motu powers for scheduled offences without state consent — match B with 4.
Section 6 DSPE Act governs state consent for CBI — match C with 1.
Article 142 'complete justice' power allows Supreme Court to direct CBI anywhere — match D with 3.
The correct combination is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates on the NIA–CBI distinction. Students who know that one of these agencies has suo motu powers may incorrectly assign it to CBI, especially when 'central government matters' are involved. The trap is reinforced by placing the NIA's defining attribute (suo motu power for scheduled offences) alongside CBI's more limited territorial suo motu scope, forcing students to distinguish between the two precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the comparative jurisdictional architecture of India's two premier central investigative agencies.

Correct Matches:
• A–2: CBI's suo motu power is narrow — it applies only within Union Territories and to cases involving central government employees on central premises. It cannot unilaterally enter state territory.
• B–4: The NIA Act, 2008 is the key distinction. NIA can suo motu take up any 'scheduled offence' (terrorism, UAPA cases, etc.) without state consent — a power CBI does not possess.
• C–1: Section 6 of the DSPE Act is the consent provision. Every CBI entry into state territory must be preceded by state consent (general or specific) unless overridden by a court.
• D–3: Article 142 grants the Supreme Court the power to pass such orders as are necessary for 'complete justice' — this has been used repeatedly to direct CBI investigations regardless of state consent (e.g., Vineet Narain, Coal Scam).

Value Addition:
• NIA's suo motu power was a deliberate legislative design choice post-26/11 Mumbai attacks to avoid federalism-based delays in terror investigations.
• CBI requires Section 3 notification + Section 6 consent; NIA requires neither for its scheduled offences.
• High Courts under Article 226 can also direct CBI investigations within their territorial jurisdiction — a lesser-known but frequently tested point.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 142 CBI direction and CVC superintendence distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, leading students to assume the most complete-sounding option is right without testing whether R actually explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Supreme Court under Article 142 can direct CBI to investigate irrespective of state consent, as established in multiple judgments including Vineet Narain.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. CVC Act 2003 does grant CVC superintendence over CBI, but only in matters relating to PC Act offences — not all CBI cases.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The Supreme Court's power under Article 142 to override state consent is derived from the Constitution itself, not from CVC's supervisory role. These are entirely separate legal provisions with no causal link.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question uses the reversed-causation trap in a subtle way. Both facts are true, which makes option (a) feel safe. However, the CVC's superintendence over CBI in anti-corruption matters is a completely separate legal provision from the Supreme Court's Article 142 power. Students who quickly verify both facts as true and select (a) without testing the causal link will be misled. The CVC's role has no bearing on why the Supreme Court can override state consent.
solution.final_explanation:
This assertion-reason tests whether students can distinguish between two simultaneously true but causally unrelated facts about CBI oversight.

Assertion (A) Analysis: Correct. Article 142 grants the Supreme Court the power to make any order necessary for 'complete justice.' Courts have repeatedly invoked this — along with Article 226 for High Courts — to direct CBI investigations even in states that have not given consent. The Vineet Narain case (1997) is the landmark that crystallised this principle.

Reason (R) Analysis: Correct but limited. Under the CVC Act, 2003, the Central Vigilance Commission exercises superintendence over CBI only in PC Act-related matters. For special crimes and economic offences, CBI answers to the Ministry of Personnel — not the CVC.

Causal Link: There is none. The Supreme Court's Article 142 power is constitutionally derived and applies to all CBI investigations. The CVC's role is confined to anti-corruption supervision and has no bearing on the court's override of the consent requirement.

Value Addition:
• Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) introduced the concept of 'Continuance Mandamus' — keeping supervision active till investigation completes.
• Article 226 High Court power is territorial; Article 142 Supreme Court power is nationwide.
• CVC superintendence explicitly excludes special crime and economic offence investigations handled by CBI.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI Director appointment and tenure — chronological reforms
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know the Vineet Narain judgment and the Lokpal Act are involved may place them in logical rather than actual chronological sequence, mistakenly reversing 1997 and 2014.
elimination_logic: Vineet Narain judgment fixed CBI Director's 2-year tenure — this is 1997. Place it first.
DSPE Amendment Act implementing collegium-type appointment (PM + LoP + CJI) came after the Lokpal Act 2013 — this is 2014. Place it second.
The 2021 amendment allowing extensions up to 5 years is the most recent development. Place it third.
Correct sequence: Vineet Narain 1997 → DSPE Amendment 2014 → Extension amendment 2021 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works here because students know all three events but may confuse whether the Lokpal Act or the DSPE Amendment came first, or whether the tenure extension came before the collegium appointment mechanism. The 2014 DSPE Amendment and 2021 extension amendments are close in time and relate to the same office, creating fertile ground for sequence errors.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal safeguards surrounding the CBI Director's appointment evolved through three distinct reform moments.

Correct Sequence: Vineet Narain Judgment (1997) → DSPE Amendment Act (2014) → Extension Amendment (2021)

• Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997): The Supreme Court, concerned about political interference in the Hawala scandal investigation, fixed the CBI Director's minimum tenure at 2 years — the first structural insulation measure.
• DSPE Amendment Act (2014): Following the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, the amendment changed the appointment mechanism to a high-powered committee: Prime Minister + Leader of Opposition + Chief Justice of India. This collegium approach was designed to depoliticise the selection.
• 2021 Amendment: Allowed annual extensions of the Director's tenure beyond 2 years, up to a maximum of 5 years — a controversial change criticised as potentially enabling political manipulation.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) places 2014 before 1997 — factually impossible.
• Option (b) reverses 1997 and 2014 — a common confusion.
• Option (d) places 2021 before 2014 — chronologically impossible.

Value Addition:
• Removal of the CBI Director requires intimation to the appointment committee — it cannot be done unilaterally by the executive.
• The LoP requirement for the appointment committee created a brief constitutional problem when no LoP was officially recognised in the Lok Sabha.
• Similar tenure protection exists for the ED Director post the 2021 amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: PC Act 2018 amendment — prior sanction for arrest
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the pre-2018 PC Act know that prior sanction was required for prosecution, and may apply the older rule without knowing the 2018 amendment extended the requirement to arrest itself.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: can a DSP-rank CBI officer arrest a serving IAS officer without any sanction?
Post-2018 PC Act amendment, prior sanction is required even for arrest of public servants — not just prosecution. Eliminate options that only require sanction at prosecution stage.
The PC Act requires DSP-rank or above for PC Act investigation — the officer's rank satisfies the Section 17 requirement. The remaining issue is arrest sanction.
The legally correct answer requires the officer to obtain prior sanction before arrest — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 2018 amendment to the PC Act is a major temporal-swap trap. Before 2018, prior sanction was needed only for prosecution. Students who studied PC Act before 2018 or from older materials will apply the older rule and conclude sanction is needed only at prosecution stage, making option (a) feel correct. The 2018 amendment fundamentally changed operational CBI practice by extending the sanction requirement to the arrest stage itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 significantly altered how CBI can act against public servants.

Applicable Principle: Under the PC Act, 1988 as amended in 2018, a prior sanction from the competent authority is now required not only for prosecution but also for the arrest of a public servant. This was a major shift from the pre-2018 position.

Scenario Analysis: A DSP-rank CBI officer satisfies the Section 17 requirement (rank of DSP or above for PC Act investigations). However, before arresting the IAS officer, the officer must obtain prior sanction from the competent authority — typically the Central Government for IAS officers.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This reflects the pre-2018 position. Sanction for prosecution was sufficient under the original act, but the 2018 amendment added the arrest sanction requirement.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: A DSP-rank officer satisfies Section 17; rank is not the obstacle here.
• Option (c) — Correct: Both the rank requirement (satisfied) and the prior sanction for arrest (required post-2018 amendment) are met only when sanction is obtained before proceeding.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: State consent is irrelevant here — IAS officers work for the Central Government, placing this squarely within CBI's central jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• The 2018 amendment also introduced a 2-year time limit for completing PC Act trials to reduce pendency.
• The sanction requirement applies to current public servants; retired officials require sanction too but from a different authority.
• Section 19 PC Act governs prosecution sanction; the arrest sanction was newly inserted via the 2018 amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI under Ministry of Personnel — not Ministry of Home Affairs
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because NIA is under the Ministry of Home Affairs, and students familiar with police/security agencies may assume CBI also falls under MHA, making them doubt the correct odd-one-out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: which ministry do these bodies report to?
NIA, IB, and NATGRID all fall under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

CBI is the odd one out — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic entity-swap trap. CBI is universally associated with law enforcement and investigation — the same domain as NIA and IB — so students instinctively group all four together under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The fact that CBI reports to the Ministry of Personnel is a frequently tested and frequently missed distinction. A partially-prepared student will eliminate NATGRID as the 'odd' technical agency without scrutinising the ministry classification.
solution.final_explanation:
The common attribute tested here is the parent ministry of India's central investigative/intelligence agencies.

• Option (a) NIA: National Investigation Agency falls under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
• Option (b) IB (Intelligence Bureau): Also under the Ministry of Home Affairs — India's domestic intelligence agency.
• Option (c) NATGRID: National Intelligence Grid, established for inter-agency data sharing, also operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs framework.
• Option (d) CBI: The odd one out. CBI is placed under the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), which falls under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions — headed by the Prime Minister.

Value Addition:
• CBI's placement under the Ministry of Personnel rather than Home Affairs is a frequently exploited UPSC distinction.
• The CVC exercises superintendence over CBI only for PC Act cases; for other matters, it is the Ministry of Personnel.
• ED (Enforcement Directorate) is under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance — another commonly confused ministry assignment.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know CVC supervises CBI may not know this is limited to PC Act cases, causing them to accept Statement 1 as wholly correct.

Statement 2 accurately identifies BSFC under CBI's Economic Offences Division for large bank frauds. Mark Statement 2 correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 is subtle. Students know CVC supervises CBI — this is a standard fact. The false element is 'all categories.' By extending CVC's real but limited role to cover all CBI cases, the statement becomes incorrect. Students who do not know that special crimes and economic offences fall under Ministry of Personnel supervision will accept Statement 1 without hesitation.
solution.final_explanation:
Two independently verifiable facts about CBI's internal structure and external oversight are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The CVC Act, 2003 limits CVC's superintendence to offences investigated under the Prevention of Corruption Act. For CBI's Special Crimes Division (terrorism, organised crime) and Economic Offences Division, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the supervisory authority. The word 'all' makes this statement false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CBI's Economic Offences Division houses the Banking Securities Fraud Cell (BSFC), which is specifically mandated to investigate large-scale bank fraud and securities market manipulation — reflecting CBI's role alongside the ED and SFIO in financial crime.

Value Addition:
• The Vineet Narain judgment (1997) suggested CVC as a buffer between CBI and the political executive — but only for corruption matters.
• For PC Act cases, the CVC can call for records, examine files, and issue directions — but cannot interfere in day-to-day investigation.
• SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office) under the Companies Act, 2013 overlaps with CBI's economic offence jurisdiction in corporate fraud cases.

solution.final_explanation:

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students know SFIO investigates corporate fraud and assume it operates under the same PMLA framework as the ED, conflating two distinct statutes.
elimination_logic: CBI investigates under IPC/CrPC — criminal investigation framework. Eliminate any pair that assigns PMLA to CBI.
ED operates under PMLA and FEMA — money laundering and foreign exchange. Pair (a) correctly assigns both statutes to ED.
SFIO operates under Companies Act 2013 — not PMLA. Eliminate pair (c) which conflates SFIO with PMLA.
Pair (a) — ED with PMLA and FEMA — is correctly matched. Select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges SFIO and ED in the student's mind — both investigate financial crimes, but under completely different statutes. Students who know ED investigates money laundering and SFIO handles corporate fraud may incorrectly assign PMLA to SFIO, especially since PMLA can apply to proceeds of corporate fraud. The correct attribution requires knowing that SFIO's exclusive legal basis is the Companies Act, 2013.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal framework each agency operates under is as important as what it investigates.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) is correctly paired with PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) and FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act). These are its two primary statutory instruments — one for money laundering (criminal) and one for foreign exchange violations (civil).
• Option (b) — Incorrect: CBI's primary framework is the IPC and CrPC for criminal investigation, plus the PC Act for corruption — not PMLA. Assigning PMLA to CBI is a conflation error.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office) derives its authority from the Companies Act, 2013 — not PMLA. While SFIO and ED may investigate the same underlying corporate fraud, they use different statutes.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CBI's jurisdiction in corruption cases comes from the PC Act, not the Companies Act. The Companies Act is SFIO's domain.

Value Addition:
• An accused can face simultaneous CBI (IPC/PC Act) and ED (PMLA) proceedings for the same underlying act — this 'twin investigation' is constitutionally permissible.
• SFIO has powers of search, seizure, and arrest under the Companies Act, 2013, making it more potent than it was before.
• MoU between CBI and ED facilitates information sharing, though jurisdictional conflicts persist.

solution.concept_anchor: Lokpal Act — CBI relationship and Section 26 powers

statement_analysis.statement: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 created a mechanism through which Lokpal can refer cases to the CBI and direct it to conduct preliminary inquiries against public servants.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 26 of the Lokpal Act authorises Lokpal to direct CBI to conduct preliminary inquiries in cases involving public servants — this is an accurate description of the referral mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 established that the CBI's prosecution wing must be separated from its investigation wing as a mandatory structural reform.
statement_analysis.reason: Separation of prosecution and investigation wings is a Law Commission recommendation and a policy debate — it has not been enacted as a mandatory requirement under the Lokpal Act.

statement_analysis.statement: The amendment to the DSPE Act following the Lokpal Act changed the CBI Director's appointment process to include the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and Chief Justice of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Lokpal Act, the DSPE Amendment Act 2014 inserted this three-member appointment committee, depoliticising the selection of the CBI Director.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who recall debates about CBI's prosecution independence may assume the Lokpal Act enacted this reform, when in fact it remains a recommendation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 accurately describes Section 26 of the Lokpal Act — Lokpal can refer cases and direct preliminary inquiries. Mark correct.
Statement 2 claims mandatory separation of prosecution and investigation — this is a Law Commission recommendation, not a Lokpal Act provision. Mark incorrect.
Statement 3 correctly identifies the three-member appointment committee (PM + LoP + CJI) created via DSPE Amendment after Lokpal Act. Mark correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the partial-truth technique by embedding a real policy debate within a factually incorrect claim about legislative enactment. The debate about separating CBI's prosecution and investigation wings is real, frequently discussed, and recommended by the Law Commission — but it has never been enacted into law. Students who follow policy debates and reforms may mistake the recommendation for actual law.
solution.final_explanation:
The Lokpal Act's relationship with CBI is a nuanced area combining direct statutory provisions with ongoing reform debates.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 26 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 empowers Lokpal to authorise CBI to conduct preliminary inquiries and to require CBI to report progress on cases referred by it.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No provision of the Lokpal Act mandates the structural separation of CBI's prosecution and investigation wings. This separation has been recommended by the Law Commission and discussed in Parliamentary committees, but remains unimplemented. Confusing recommendation with enactment is a common examination error.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The DSPE (Amendment) Act, 2014 — enacted in the legislative wake of the Lokpal Act — introduced the three-member appointment committee comprising the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and Chief Justice of India.

Value Addition:
• CBI must submit progress reports to Lokpal on cases referred under Section 26 — adding a layer of accountability.
• The Law Commission in its 24th Report recommended an independent prosecution directorate for CBI.
• When there is no recognized Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the leader of the single largest opposition party has sometimes been considered as a substitute.

solution.concept_anchor: Caged Parrot observation — Coal Scam 2013
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the Vineet Narain case (1997) is the more famous CBI-related Supreme Court judgment, and students who associate major CBI judicial observations with Vineet Narain will incorrectly select it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate the Vineet Narain case — it dealt with Hawala scandal investigation and established Continuance Mandamus, not the 'caged parrot' metaphor.
The 'caged parrot' observation arose from CBI sharing status reports with the Law Ministry/PMO in the Coal Scam — this was 2013.
Eliminate the 2G Spectrum case — a different investigation with different judicial observations.
Confirm: Coal Scam case (2013) is where the Supreme Court used this specific characterization — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the student's tendency to associate major CBI judicial observations with the more famous Vineet Narain judgment (1997). Both cases involve Supreme Court supervision of CBI, making them easy to conflate. The 'caged parrot' metaphor is specific to the Coal Scam proceedings of 2013, where the court reacted to the sharing of CBI's investigation status report with political functionaries.
solution.final_explanation:
The 'caged parrot speaking in its master's voice' is one of the Supreme Court's most striking characterisations of the CBI's structural vulnerability.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1997) dealt with the Hawala scandal and established the doctrine of 'Continuance Mandamus' and the 2-year tenure for the CBI Director — not the 'caged parrot' metaphor.
• Option (b) — Correct: In 2013, during the Coal Block Allocation Scam hearing, the Supreme Court used this phrase after discovering that CBI had shared its investigation status report with the Law Ministry and PMO — entities that could influence the course of investigation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 2G Spectrum case involved CBI investigation of telecom corruption but did not produce the 'caged parrot' observation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Hawala Case is another name for Vineet Narain — already eliminated.

Value Addition:
• The court directed that CBI must not share investigation reports with accused persons or the political executive in the Coal Scam case.
• This observation renewed demands for a dedicated CBI Act to insulate the agency structurally.
• Structural reforms suggested included an independent prosecution directorate and fixed tenure for all senior CBI officials.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI as Interpol NCB — extradition via MEA not CBI

statement_analysis.statement: CBI serves as India's National Central Bureau (NCB) for Interpol and coordinates international criminal intelligence sharing.
statement_analysis.reason: CBI is India's designated NCB for Interpol, making it the nodal point for all Interpol-related coordination including Red Notices and intelligence sharing.

statement_analysis.statement: Formal extradition requests from foreign governments are processed directly by the CBI as the nodal Interpol agency.
statement_analysis.reason: While CBI coordinates MLATs, formal extradition requests are processed through the Ministry of External Affairs — not directly by CBI.

statement_analysis.statement: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 empowers only the Enforcement Directorate to attach assets of economic fugitives — CBI has no role under this Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Both CBI and ED can attach assets under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 — the act is not exclusive to the ED.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 (CBI as NCB for Interpol) is a genuine fact that students may doubt if they confuse it with the MEA's role in international cooperation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is accurate — CBI is India's NCB for Interpol. This is correct, so it should NOT be marked as incorrect.
Statement 2 claims CBI processes formal extradition requests directly — this is incorrect. MEA handles extradition. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3 claims only ED can act under FEOA 2018 — this is incorrect. CBI also has powers under this Act. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 is the central deception: students know CBI is the Interpol nodal body and may naturally extend this to all international cooperation including extradition. However, extradition is a sovereign matter processed through the Ministry of External Affairs. CBI's Interpol role is for criminal intelligence and Mutual Legal Assistance — not for formal extradition requests.
solution.final_explanation:
India's international criminal cooperation framework involves multiple agencies with distinct roles.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CBI's designation as India's NCB for Interpol makes it the operational hub for Red Notices, diffusions, and bilateral criminal intelligence sharing under the Interpol framework.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (NOT correct): Formal extradition requests involve diplomatic processes governed by bilateral extradition treaties and processed through the Ministry of External Affairs. CBI's MLAT coordination is for evidence and information sharing — not extradition per se.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (NOT correct): The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 allows both CBI and ED to initiate proceedings to attach and confiscate assets of economic fugitives. It is not exclusive to the ED. This Act supplements (but does not replace) the extradition mechanism.

Value Addition:
• India has bilateral extradition treaties with over 40 countries; the UK, USA, and UAE are among the most frequently invoked.
• Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) are used to obtain evidence and witness cooperation — CBI coordinates these requests.
• The FEOA 2018 was enacted following high-profile cases of economic offenders fleeing India — it allows confiscation without extradition in some circumstances.

solution.concept_anchor: State withdrawal of consent — West Bengal 2010 SC judgment

statement_analysis.statement: 'Police' as a subject falls under Entry 2 of List II (State List) in the Seventh Schedule, which is the constitutional basis for requiring state consent for CBI operations.
statement_analysis.reason: Entry 2 of List II places police under state jurisdiction, which is the constitutional foundation for the Section 6 consent requirement — CBI cannot override this without judicial or constitutional backing.

statement_analysis.statement: The DSPE Act is constitutionally valid because it is legislated under Entry 80 of List I (Union List), which covers the extension of powers of central police forces to states.
statement_analysis.reason: Entry 80, List I specifically covers extension of powers and jurisdiction of central police forces, validating the DSPE Act as a Union legislation without violating the state's police power.

statement_analysis.statement: In State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010), the Supreme Court held that a High Court cannot direct CBI to investigate in a state that has withdrawn its general consent.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court held the opposite — that a High Court can direct CBI to investigate in a state even if that state has withdrawn general consent, as constitutional courts' powers cannot be fettered by state executive decisions.

statement_analysis.statement: West Bengal, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Kerala are among the states that have formally withdrawn their general consent to CBI investigations.
statement_analysis.reason: These four states are the well-documented examples of states that have withdrawn general consent, creating jurisdictional complexities for pending and future CBI investigations in those states.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who know the West Bengal 2010 case involved CBI consent issues may misremember the court's ruling and accept Statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correctly identifies Entry 2, List II as the police jurisdiction basis — correct.
Statement 2 correctly invokes Entry 80, List I for DSPE Act validity — correct.
Statement 3 states the High Court CANNOT direct CBI in a non-consenting state — this reverses the actual ruling. The SC held High Courts CAN direct CBI despite withdrawn consent. Mark incorrect.
Statement 4 correctly lists states that have withdrawn consent — correct.
Three of four correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a geographic-swap variant: it correctly names the case (State of West Bengal 2010) and the facts (withdrawn consent) but reverses the holding. Students who know this landmark case was about CBI consent in West Bengal may accept the statement without scrutinising whether the court ruled for or against the High Court's power. The case is famous precisely because the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's power to direct CBI despite withdrawn consent.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional foundations of CBI's federal jurisdiction require understanding multiple Seventh Schedule entries.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Police' under Entry 2, List II is the bedrock of states' resistance to CBI operations without consent. This entry gives states plenary power over police functions.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Entry 80, List I ('extension of powers and jurisdiction of members of a police force belonging to one State to another State') validates the DSPE Act without violating the state police power.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010) held precisely the opposite — that constitutional courts (High Courts and Supreme Court) can direct CBI investigation regardless of whether a state has withdrawn its general consent. Executive withdrawals cannot fetter constitutional court powers.
• Statement 4 — Correct: West Bengal, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Kerala have formally withdrawn general consent — a significant federal development with real operational consequences for CBI.

Value Addition:
• The 2010 West Bengal case is a landmark on the federal limits of state consent withdrawal.
• Cases already registered before consent withdrawal continue unaffected — the withdrawal is prospective.
• Article 355 (Centre's duty to protect states) has occasionally been invoked in debates about CBI's federal role.

solution.concept_anchor: Courts cannot direct CBI beyond Section 3 notified offences
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both the fact of High Court power under Article 226 and the Section 3 limitation are individually known to prepared students, but they may not connect the causal relationship correctly — assuming Article 226 power fully explains the Section 3 limit.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Courts (High Courts under Article 226, Supreme Court under Articles 32/142) can direct CBI to investigate irrespective of state consent. This is settled law.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Courts cannot direct CBI to investigate offences not notified under Section 3 of the DSPE Act — the subject-matter jurisdiction is a hard limit even for constitutional courts.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The reason courts can override state consent derives from their constitutional supremacy under Articles 226 and 142, not from the Section 3 notification mechanism. R describes a separate and independent limitation on court power, not the explanation for why courts can override state consent.

Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (c) ... Wait — re-checking: A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option (b). Let me re-verify: The standard mapping: A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A = option (b). Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question traps students who correctly identify both facts but do not test the causal link. Assertion A (courts can override state consent) and Reason R (courts cannot direct CBI beyond Section 3 notified offences) are both true. But R describes an independent limitation on court power — it does not explain why courts can override state consent. The scope-extension trap lies in the implicit suggestion that the Section 3 framework 'governs' the court's power, when in fact the court's override power derives purely from the Constitution.
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires careful separation of two true but causally unrelated facts about judicial power over CBI.

Assertion (A) Analysis: Correct. High Courts under Article 226 and the Supreme Court under Articles 32 and 142 can direct CBI to investigate cases regardless of whether a state has given or withdrawn consent. Constitutional court powers are not subordinate to executive state decisions under Section 6.

Reason (R) Analysis: Correct. Even constitutional courts cannot order CBI to investigate offences that have not been notified under Section 3 of the DSPE Act. Subject-matter jurisdiction is a hard statutory limit — courts cannot expand CBI's investigative remit by order.

Causal Link: R does not explain A. The court's power to override state consent (A) flows from Articles 226, 32, and 142 of the Constitution. The Section 3 notification limit (R) is a separate, independent constraint on what CBI can investigate — it restricts the scope of court directions but does not explain the source of the court's authority to override consent.

Value Addition:
• Both limits — Section 3 (what CBI can investigate) and Section 6 (where CBI can investigate) — are independent of each other.
• A court can override Section 6 (consent) but cannot override Section 3 (notification) — this asymmetry is the key examination point.
• Vineet Narain established that CBI must be independent from political executive — but courts themselves remain a check.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 3 DSPE — notification prerequisite for CBI jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it sounds constitutionally grounded — suggesting CBI can investigate anything involving central government — but this misses the notification prerequisite under Section 3.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option suggesting CBI has blanket jurisdiction over all central government matters — Section 3 requires specific notification.
Eliminate options claiming CBI's jurisdiction is defined by court orders alone — courts cannot expand Section 3 notified offences.
The correct principle is that Central Government must notify specific offences via executive order — this is mandatory, not discretionary.
Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by presenting an attractive broad formulation — 'CBI can investigate all matters concerning the Central Government' — which sounds plausible given CBI's role as the premier central investigative agency. The reality is narrower: Section 3 requires specific notification of each category of offences, and CBI cannot automatically investigate a central government matter simply because the Centre is involved.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 3 of the DSPE Act is the gatekeeping provision for CBI's subject-matter jurisdiction.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: CBI does not have automatic jurisdiction over all matters involving central government employees or property. The scope-extension makes this false — the notification mechanism is mandatory.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Central Government must specifically notify the offences that CBI is empowered to investigate. This notification can be expanded or contracted by executive order, giving the government flexibility to include emerging crime types like cybercrime or contract specific categories.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Parliamentary legislation can influence the framework, but Section 3 specifically operates through executive notification — not direct Parliamentary action for each offence category.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CBI's jurisdiction is not self-determined. It cannot unilaterally declare its own investigative remit — the notification must come from the Central Government.

Value Addition:
• Currently notified offences include PC Act corruption, economic offences, bank fraud, and conventional serious crimes of national importance.
• The notification mechanism is the executive's tool to both empower and limit CBI — a significant concentration of power.
• Courts cannot use Article 226 or 142 to direct CBI on non-notified offences — subject-matter jurisdiction is an absolute limit.

solution.concept_anchor: PC Act Section 17 rank requirement and 2018 arrest sanction amendment

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 17 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, a CBI officer must hold at least the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) to investigate offences under the Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 17 of the PC Act specifies that only a DSP-rank or above officer can investigate PC Act offences — this is a statutory rank requirement that directly governs CBI's investigative operations.

statement_analysis.statement: The original Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 required prior sanction both for the arrest and for the prosecution of a public servant.
statement_analysis.reason: The original 1988 Act required prior sanction only for prosecution — the requirement for sanction before arrest was introduced only by the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018.

statement_analysis.statement: Special Courts designated for CBI cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act are appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the relevant High Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Special Judges for PC Act/CBI cases are appointed through this consultation mechanism — they are not regular sessions court judges and are not appointed independently by the High Court.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct, creating a false comfort that the entire set must be correct — students may overlook the temporal error in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Section 17 PC Act — DSP rank or above required for investigation. This is correct and well-established.

Statement 2: Claims original 1988 Act required arrest sanction — this is the temporal-swap trap. Arrest sanction was added only in 2018. The original act only required prosecution sanction. Mark incorrect.
Statement 3: Central Government + High Court consultation for Special Judge appointment is accurate. Mark correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a temporal-swap to make the post-2018 amendment appear as if it was part of the original 1988 Act. Students who are aware of the 2018 amendment (arrest sanction requirement) and the 1988 Act (prosecution sanction) may not carefully distinguish whether the arrest sanction was always present or was added in 2018. The statement sounds plausible because both sanction requirements exist now, but the 'original 1988' specification makes it incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The Prevention of Corruption Act framework creates specific operational constraints for CBI that have evolved over time.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 17 is a rank-based gatekeeping provision. Only DSP-rank or above CBI officers can investigate PC Act offences — ensuring senior oversight of politically sensitive corruption cases.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The original PC Act, 1988 required prior sanction only at the prosecution stage (Section 19). The requirement to obtain sanction before making an arrest was a significant new addition introduced by the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 — it was not part of the original 1988 framework.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Special Judges under the PC Act are appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the High Court. This is a joint appointment mechanism distinct from regular sessions court appointments made by State Governments.

Value Addition:
• The 2018 amendment also added a 2-year time limit for completing trials in PC Act cases — reducing the pendency burden.
• The amendment was driven by Supreme Court concerns about misuse of arrest powers in corruption cases.
• A Special CBI Court's judgment is appealed directly to the High Court — bypassing the Sessions Court level.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI non-statutory — implications for suo motu power and reforms
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'statutory body' is associated with CBI's significant powers and national prominence — students unfamiliar with the precise legal definition of 'statutory body' may assume prominence equals statutory status.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes an agency whose name is not in any statute — only an executive resolution. Identify this as CBI's non-statutory character.
A non-statutory agency lacks inherent suo motu investigation powers — this eliminates options claiming plenary investigative authority.
The scenario asks what constitutional/legal implication flows from non-statutory status. The answer must address the dependence on consent and notification.
Option (d) correctly identifies that non-statutory status means no inherent suo motu power and dependence on DSPE Act mechanisms — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) uses plausible-fabrication: it invokes the concept of 'deemed statutory body' which has no established legal meaning in Indian administrative law. Students who conflate institutional prominence with statutory status, or who have heard the term 'deemed' used in other contexts (deemed universities, deemed forests), will find this option plausible. The correct answer requires knowing that the DSPE Act — not any CBI-specific statute — is the operative law, and the implications this has for suo motu power.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario mirrors CBI's precise legal situation — an agency whose operational name appears only in a ministerial resolution, not in any Act of Parliament.

Applicable Principle: When an agency lacks its own statute, it must operate entirely within the framework of an existing act (here, the DSPE Act). This creates specific limitations: no suo motu investigation powers in states, dependence on the notification mechanism (Section 3) for subject-matter jurisdiction, and the requirement of state consent (Section 6) for territorial jurisdiction.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Agencies without their own statute can still have significant powers — but only those explicitly granted under the applicable act. The absence of a statute does not automatically render all actions invalid.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: There is no concept of 'deemed statutory body' in Indian administrative law that elevates an executive resolution to statutory status. This is a fabricated legal concept.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Judicial recognition of an agency's functions does not cure the absence of statutory backing — courts can direct the agency but cannot create statutory powers through recognition alone.
• Option (d) — Correct: Without its own statute, the agency has no inherent investigative powers beyond those conferred by the DSPE Act. This means no suo motu state investigation, dependence on Central Government notifications, and vulnerability to political executive oversight.

Value Addition:
• The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended a dedicated CBI Act to remedy this structural gap.
• Parliamentary Standing Committees have repeatedly called for statutory independence including an independent budget for CBI.
• The FBI (US) analogy — often cited in reform debates — is imperfect since FBI operates under a different federal structure.

solution.concept_anchor: NIA Act 2008 suo motu power vs CBI Section 6 consent

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The National Investigation Agency can, suo motu, take up investigation of scheduled offences across states without requiring the consent of state governments.
statement_analysis.reason: The NIA Act, 2008 explicitly empowers NIA to investigate scheduled offences (including terrorism and UAPA cases) across state boundaries without state consent — a deliberate design to prevent state-level obstruction of terror investigations.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The Central Bureau of Investigation also has suo motu power to investigate scheduled offences under the NIA Act, 2008 since both agencies are central investigative bodies with overlapping jurisdiction in terror financing cases.
statement_analysis.reason: CBI does not derive any suo motu power from the NIA Act — CBI's powers are derived entirely from the DSPE Act, 1946. Overlapping jurisdiction in subject matter does not transfer NIA's statutory suo motu powers to CBI.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both agencies do have overlapping jurisdiction in terror financing, leading students to assume both share the same powers under the NIA Act.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: NIA Act 2008 grants suo motu power for scheduled offences. Unambiguously correct.
Statement 2 claims CBI derives suo motu power from NIA Act — CBI's legal basis is exclusively the DSPE Act. Entity-swap between CBI and NIA makes this false.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap conflates the powers of two central investigative agencies that operate in overlapping domains. Students know both NIA and CBI can investigate terror financing. The false statement exploits this overlap by suggesting CBI derives suo motu power from the NIA Act. This is factually wrong — CBI has no powers under the NIA Act and its suo motu scope is limited to Union Territories and central premises under the DSPE Act.
solution.final_explanation:
The NIA–CBI distinction on suo motu powers is one of the most frequently tested comparative points in UPSC Polity.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The NIA Act, 2008 was enacted specifically to create a central agency with nationwide suo motu power for terrorism and allied offences. 'Scheduled offences' under the NIA Act include UAPA, Explosive Substances Act, and related terrorism statutes. NIA does not need state consent.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CBI's legal powers flow entirely from the DSPE Act, 1946. The NIA Act confers powers only on NIA officers. Even where CBI and NIA have concurrent interest in a case (e.g., terror financing), CBI cannot use NIA Act powers. CBI's suo motu power is limited to Union Territories and cases involving central employees on central premises — nothing more.

Value Addition:
• NIA can supersede state police investigations in scheduled offences — a power CBI lacks entirely.
• NIA has primacy over CBI in terror-financing cases under the NIA Act schedule.
• CBI can be called in to assist or supplement NIA investigation but must still comply with Section 6 consent for state territory unless directed by a court.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 142 — complete justice power for CBI direction
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies and students associate it with Supreme Court power, but Article 32 is for enforcement of fundamental rights — the plenary 'complete justice' power resides in Article 142.
elimination_logic: The blank requires the constitutional provision that gives the Supreme Court power to issue any order for 'complete justice' — this is a distinctive phrase.
Article 32 is for enforcement of fundamental rights — not a plenary 'complete justice' power.
Article 136 is Special Leave Petition — appellate power, not original investigative direction power.
Article 142 is the 'complete justice' provision — the correct answer. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap here is between Article 32 and Article 142 — two Supreme Court powers that students frequently conflate. Article 32 gives the Court power to enforce fundamental rights through writs; Article 142 is the broader 'complete justice' provision that has been used to direct CBI investigations, restructure institutions, and override procedural constraints. Students who instinctively associate Supreme Court power with Article 32 will select it without scrutinising whether it is the correct instrument for investigative directions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court's power to direct CBI investigations irrespective of state consent rests on a specific constitutional provision.

• Option (a) Article 226 — Incorrect: Article 226 is the High Courts' writ jurisdiction. It allows High Courts to direct CBI within their territorial jurisdiction but cannot extend nationwide or override all state consent issues as comprehensively as Article 142.
• Option (b) Article 142 — Correct: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order 'as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.' This provision has been the constitutional basis for Supreme Court-directed CBI investigations in landmark cases like Vineet Narain and the Coal Scam.
• Option (c) Article 32 — Incorrect: Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies — it empowers the Supreme Court to enforce fundamental rights through writs. While it can initiate proceedings, it is Article 142 that provides the broad, plenary direction power used in investigative directions.
• Option (d) Article 136 — Incorrect: Article 136 is the Special Leave Petition provision — it is an appellate gateway, not a source of investigative direction power.

Value Addition:
• Article 142 has also been used to dissolve marriages, direct compensation, and restructure cricket boards — its scope goes well beyond CBI cases.
• Vineet Narain (1997) used Article 142 to maintain continuous supervision over CBI in the Hawala investigation.
• High Courts use Article 226 for CBI directions within their territory — the national override requires Article 142.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places CBI with IPC/CrPC but incorrectly swaps SFIO and ED frameworks, exploiting the common conflation of PMLA and Companies Act in corporate fraud investigations.
elimination_logic: CBI investigates under IPC/CrPC — the foundational criminal law framework. Match A with 3.
ED operates under PMLA 2002 (money laundering) and FEMA 1999 (foreign exchange). Match B with 1.
SFIO derives authority exclusively from Companies Act, 2013 — not PMLA. Match C with 4.
Special CBI Courts are established under PC Act and Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952. Match D with 2.
Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges SFIO and ED in the student's mental framework. Both investigate financial crime; both can act on corporate fraud. Students who know ED uses PMLA may extend this to SFIO, especially since PMLA can apply to proceeds of corporate fraud. The correct attribution requires knowing that SFIO's exclusive legal basis is Companies Act, 2013 — a distinction tested precisely because it is counterintuitive (fraud cases would seem to be money laundering cases too).
solution.final_explanation:
The legal frameworks governing India's overlapping financial crime agencies are a rich source of UPSC questions.

Correct Matches:
• A–3 (CBI → IPC/CrPC): CBI is a criminal investigation agency. Its primary legal toolkit is the Indian Penal Code for substantive offences and the Code of Criminal Procedure for investigative procedure — supplemented by the PC Act for corruption.
• B–1 (ED → PMLA and FEMA): The Enforcement Directorate has two distinct mandates: PMLA for money laundering (criminal) and FEMA for foreign exchange violations (civil/quasi-criminal). These are separate statutes targeting different aspects of financial crime.
• C–4 (SFIO → Companies Act, 2013): The Serious Fraud Investigation Office is constituted under and draws powers from the Companies Act, 2013. It handles corporate governance failures, fraud by directors, and mismanagement — not money laundering per se.
• D–2 (Special CBI Courts → PC Act + Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952): These courts are designated under both these statutes. The Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 is the older basis; the PC Act reinforced and updated the framework.

Value Addition:
• The same corporate fraud can trigger SFIO (Companies Act), CBI (IPC/CrPC), and ED (PMLA) investigations simultaneously — 'twin' or 'triple' investigation.
• SFIO can arrest, search, and seize under Companies Act — powers significantly enhanced by the 2013 version.
• Coordination between CBI and ED is governed by an MOU for information sharing, but jurisdictional conflicts remain unresolved.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI Director appointment committee and removal safeguards

statement_analysis.statement: Under the DSPE Amendment Act, 2014, the CBI Director is appointed by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2014 amendment inserted this three-member collegium-type appointment mechanism specifically to reduce executive discretion in selecting the CBI Director.

statement_analysis.statement: The CBI Director can be removed at any time at the discretion of the Central Government, provided the removal order is recorded in writing.
statement_analysis.reason: Removal of the CBI Director requires intimation to the appointment committee — it cannot be done unilaterally at executive discretion, even with a written order.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2021 amendment to the DSPE Act allows the tenure of the CBI Director to be extended annually beyond the initial 2-year term, up to a maximum total tenure of 5 years.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2021 amendment explicitly enables annual post-2-year extensions, permitting a total tenure of up to 5 years for the CBI Director.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is a strong distractor because the written recording requirement in Statement 2 makes the removal condition sound sufficiently formal and procedural to satisfy students who know executive power has some limits on removal.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: PM + LoP + CJI committee for appointment — correctly describes the 2014 amendment. Mark correct.

Statement 2: 'At any time at the discretion of the Central Government' — removal requires intimation to the appointment committee, not mere executive discretion. The partial-truth of 'written order' does not save the false claim of unchecked discretion. Mark incorrect.
Statement 3: Annual extensions up to 5 years total — correctly describes the 2021 amendment. Mark correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth construction: the written recording requirement sounds like a meaningful safeguard, lending false legitimacy to the claim of executive discretion. Students who know removal is not entirely at will but require some formality may accept 'written order' as a sufficient constraint. The real safeguard — intimation to and involvement of the appointment committee — is more robust than a mere written record, and this distinction makes Statement 2 incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The CBI Director's appointment and removal safeguards represent one of India's most debated institutional independence mechanisms.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2014 DSPE Amendment, enacted in the context of the Lokpal Act, introduced the three-member collegium: PM (chair), Leader of Opposition (Lok Sabha), and Chief Justice of India. This was directly inspired by the Vineet Narain recommendation for insulation from political executive.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The executive cannot remove the CBI Director unilaterally, even with a written order. The removal requires intimation to the appointment committee — a critical safeguard that adds a layer of institutional check on executive whim.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2021 amendment was controversial because it extended potential tenure from a fixed 2 years to up to 5 years through annual extensions — critics argued this could actually increase rather than reduce political influence by making extension-seeking Directors more pliable.

Value Addition:
• Similar 5-year extension provisions were simultaneously applied to the Enforcement Directorate Director in 2021.
• The LoP slot in the appointment committee was contested when the largest opposition party did not officially qualify for LoP status in certain Lok Sabha compositions.
• Post-Vineet Narain, fixed tenure was designed to prevent 'midnight transfers' of CBI Directors — a pre-1997 practice.

solution.concept_anchor: Vineet Narain — CVC as buffer and political executive oversight
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who correctly verify both facts as true may doubt whether the CVC's limited supervisory role really explains the political insulation concern, mistakenly selecting 'both correct but R not the explanation.'
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Vineet Narain judgment (1997) specifically directed that the CVC should serve as a buffer between the CBI and the political executive in anti-corruption matters, reducing direct executive control.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. CVC superintendence is limited to PC Act offences — it does not extend to all CBI investigations. This limitation is directly stated in the CVC Act, 2003.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Vineet Narain judgment placed CVC as a supervisory buffer precisely because the Court wanted a non-political body to oversee anti-corruption investigations. The CVC's limited superintendence (confined to PC Act cases) is the structural mechanism through which this insulation operates — R explains the scope and rationale of A.
Both A and R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Vineet Narain judgment created the CVC-as-buffer model specifically for anti-corruption investigations.

Assertion (A) Analysis: Correct. The 1997 Supreme Court judgment in Vineet Narain v. Union of India was a watershed moment. Concerned by the political executive's influence over CBI in the Hawala scandal, the Court directed that the CVC should exercise superintendence over CBI in corruption-related investigations — creating an institutional buffer between CBI and the Ministry.

Reason (R) Analysis: Correct. The CVC Act, 2003 codified this by limiting CVC's superintendence to offences under the PC Act. For other categories (special crimes, economic offences), the Ministry of Personnel remains the oversight authority.

Causal Relationship: R explains A. The CVC's limited superintendence is the implementation mechanism of the insulation the Court sought in Vineet Narain. By placing CVC — a statutory, non-partisan body — as the supervisor for corruption cases, the Court reduced the space for political executive interference. The limitation to PC Act cases is not a gap but a deliberate delineation.

Value Addition:
• Vineet Narain also introduced 'Continuance Mandamus' — a continuing court order keeping supervision alive until investigation completes.
• The CVC is a statutory body under the CVC Act, 2003 — appointed by PM + Home Minister + LoP.
• The Coal Scam 'caged parrot' observation (2013) suggested even the CVC buffer was insufficient — executive influence had persisted.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI legislative and institutional timeline — DSPE to Lokpal
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may place the 1963 Home Ministry Resolution after the Vineet Narain judgment, confusing the chronology by associating CBI's name with its judicial recognition rather than its administrative creation.
elimination_logic: DSPE Act was enacted in 1946 during British India for wartime corruption — this is the earliest event. Place it first.
Home Ministry Resolution conferring the name 'CBI' was issued in 1963 — after independence and DSPE Act. Place it second.
Vineet Narain judgment (1997) fixed 2-year tenure and CVC buffer — this is well after 1963. Place it third.
Lokpal Act 2013 with DSPE Amendment 2014 is the most recent. Place it fourth.
Correct sequence: DSPE Act 1946 → HM Resolution 1963 → Vineet Narain 1997 → Lokpal/DSPE Amendment 2013-14 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap operates on the 1963 Home Ministry Resolution — a fact that students often learn in conjunction with CBI's modern context and therefore mentally place closer to the 1990s judicial reforms than its actual 1963 date. Students who conflate the creation of CBI's name with judicial recognition of its independence may reverse the 1963 and 1997 positions.
solution.final_explanation:
The institutional evolution of CBI spans nearly eight decades of Indian legal and political history.

Correct Sequence: DSPE Act (1946) → Home Ministry Resolution (1963) → Vineet Narain Judgment (1997) → Lokpal Act / DSPE Amendment (2013–14)

• DSPE Act, 1946: The foundational statute, enacted for wartime corruption investigations, continued post-independence under Article 372.
• Home Ministry Resolution, 1963: This resolution formally created the name 'Central Bureau of Investigation' — the agency's identity in common parlance. It has no statutory force but has been consistently recognized.
• Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997: The landmark Supreme Court judgment that fixed the 2-year minimum tenure for the CBI Director and established the CVC buffer against political executive interference.
• Lokpal Act 2013 / DSPE Amendment 2014: The most recent legislative reform wave — introduced the collegium appointment mechanism (PM + LoP + CJI) for the CBI Director.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) places 1963 before 1946 — impossible.
• Option (c) reverses 1963 and 1997 — the common temporal-swap trap.
• Option (d) places Vineet Narain before the 1963 Resolution — impossible.

Value Addition:
• The DSPE Act predates the Constitution — one of few operational laws from the pre-independence era still in active use.
• The 2021 extension amendment is the most recent addition to this chronology.
• Understanding this timeline helps place each reform in its political context — each was a reaction to a specific governance crisis.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI Anti-Corruption Division — PC Act central employees jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because bank fraud is a financial crime that students associate with corruption, making it seem like a natural CBI Anti-Corruption Division case — but large bank frauds are handled by the Economic Offences Division.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: which of these case types belongs to the CBI's Anti-Corruption Division (ACD)?
PC Act cases against central government employees — ACD jurisdiction.
Bribery cases involving central government public servants — ACD jurisdiction.
Disproportionate assets cases against IAS officers — ACD jurisdiction.
