Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Bank fraud cases involve financial misconduct and can involve public servants, making them feel like natural Anti-Corruption Division territory. The entity-swap trap exploits this intuition by placing a legitimate Economic Offences Division function alongside three genuine ACD functions. Students who do not know that CBI's three divisions — Anti-Corruption, Special Crimes, and Economic Offences — have distinct mandates will fail to identify the odd one out.
solution.final_explanation:
CBI's three operational divisions have non-overlapping functional mandates.

• Option (a) — ACD jurisdiction: Cases under the PC Act involving central government employees are the core mandate of the Anti-Corruption Division. This is the division's defining function.
• Option (b) — ACD jurisdiction: Bribery cases against central public servants fall squarely within ACD's remit — these are Regular Cases (RCs) in CBI terminology.
• Option (c) — NOT ACD jurisdiction: Large-value bank fraud cases are handled by the Banking Securities Fraud Cell (BSFC) within CBI's Economic Offences Division (EOD), not the Anti-Corruption Division. This is the odd one out.
• Option (d) — ACD jurisdiction: Disproportionate assets (DA) investigations against IAS or other central service officers are a key ACD function — these are corruption cases under the PC Act.

Value Addition:
• CBI's three main divisions: Anti-Corruption Division (ACD), Special Crimes Division (SCD), and Economic Offences Division (EOD).
• BSFC under EOD was specifically created to handle large-value banking fraud after major bank scams in the 1990s.
• The SCD handles terrorism, organized crime, and cases of national security importance.

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended insulating the CBI from political control through a dedicated statutory charter.
statement_analysis.reason: The Second ARC explicitly recommended a separate CBI statute to provide structural independence — this is a documented recommendation directly relevant to CBI's non-statutory status.

statement_analysis.statement: The Law Commission of India recommended the separation of CBI's investigation and prosecution wings to prevent prosecutorial influence on investigation outcomes.
statement_analysis.reason: The Law Commission recommended this separation in its reports, identifying the integration of investigation and prosecution within CBI as a conflict-of-interest risk.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary Standing Committee recommendations include time-bound investigations, independent budget allocation for CBI, and statutory backing.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary Standing Committees have consistently called for all three reforms — time-bound investigations, ring-fenced budget independent of Ministry discretion, and a dedicated CBI statute.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Police Commission (1977-81) recommended that CBI be placed under a statutory supervisory board including retired Supreme Court judges, similar to the FBI Oversight Board in the United States.
statement_analysis.reason: The National Police Commission's recommendations were focused on state police reforms. The specific 'statutory supervisory board including retired SC judges' modelled on the FBI Oversight Board is not an established NPC recommendation — this is a plausible-fabrication combining real entities with a fabricated proposal.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is a strong distractor because Statements 1, 2, and 3 are all correct, creating momentum toward accepting Statement 4 as well — especially since it references real bodies (NPC, Supreme Court) in a plausible institutional reform context.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Second ARC + statutory charter for CBI — documented recommendation. Mark correct.
Statement 2: Law Commission + separation of investigation and prosecution — documented recommendation. Mark correct.
Statement 3: Parliamentary Standing Committee + three specific reforms — documented calls. Mark correct.

Statement 4: National Police Commission recommending an FBI-style oversight board with retired SC judges — the NPC focused on state police reform, and this specific recommendation is fabricated. Mark incorrect.
Three of four correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 uses a sophisticated plausible-fabrication. It combines three real elements — the National Police Commission (a real body), retired Supreme Court judges (a real oversight mechanism used elsewhere in India), and the FBI Oversight Board (a real US institution) — into a proposal that sounds exactly like something an institutional reform body would recommend. Students who cannot recall whether NPC made this specific recommendation will be attracted by its institutional plausibility.
solution.final_explanation:
Reform demands around CBI's structural independence have come from multiple authoritative bodies across different decades.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-09) was explicit in recommending a dedicated CBI statute as the primary mechanism for structural independence from political executive control.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Law Commission identified the dual role of CBI — as both investigator and de facto prosecutor — as a structural conflict. Separation would allow each wing to operate independently, reducing pressure on investigators from prosecution considerations.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Parliamentary Standing Committees on Home Affairs and Personnel have consistently flagged three reform priorities: time-bound investigations (to address pendency), independent budget allocation (to reduce Ministry leverage), and statutory backing (to cure the DSPE Act limitation).
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The National Police Commission (1977-81) focused primarily on state police reform — issues like police accountability, oversight boards, and separation of law and order from investigation at the state level. A specific recommendation for a CBI supervisory board modelled on the FBI Oversight Board is a fabricated proposal with no basis in NPC reports.

Value Addition:
• The FBI comparison is frequently used in reform debates but is constitutionally imperfect — India's federal structure differs from the US model.
• NHRC, CVC, and Lokpal all have statutory backing — CBI's lack of its own statute remains a structural anomaly among major national institutions.
• Independent budget for CBI would require it to seek its own Parliamentary allocation rather than routing through the Ministry of Personnel.

solution.concept_anchor: High Court Article 226 — territorial limit on CBI directions
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know courts can direct CBI and override state consent may assume this power is nationwide for all courts, extending the High Court's territorial jurisdiction without scrutiny.
elimination_logic: High Courts exercise jurisdiction under Article 226 within their territorial limits — this is a foundational constitutional principle.
A High Court can direct CBI to investigate crimes within its territorial jurisdiction — this transfers state police cases to CBI.
However, a High Court cannot direct CBI to investigate crimes occurring entirely outside its territorial jurisdiction — that requires the Supreme Court under Articles 32/142.
The correct option identifies the territorial limitation as the key constraint — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap adds 'nationwide' to High Court jurisdiction — an attractive but incorrect extension. Students who know High Courts can direct CBI may not carefully check whether the word 'nationwide' is accurate. In reality, High Court powers under Article 226 are territorially bounded, and only the Supreme Court under Articles 32 and 142 can exercise genuinely nationwide investigative direction powers.
solution.final_explanation:
High Court powers to direct CBI are real but spatially bounded.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: High Courts cannot transfer state police investigations to CBI for cases occurring outside their territorial jurisdiction. The geographic limit is absolute under Article 226.
• Option (b) — Correct: A High Court can direct the transfer of investigation from state police to CBI for cases within its territorial jurisdiction. This is an established power exercised under Article 226. However, the territorial boundary of the High Court defines the outer limit of this power.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Courts cannot expand CBI's subject-matter jurisdiction by directing it to investigate non-notified offences. The Section 3 notification is a hard constraint even for constitutional courts.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: High Courts do not have nationwide investigative direction power — only the Supreme Court can exercise such nationwide authority under Articles 32 and 142.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court's Article 142 power is the only constitutional instrument for nationwide CBI investigative directions.
• State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010) confirmed High Court power to direct CBI even when the state has withdrawn consent — but only within the High Court's territory.
• Frequent court-directed CBI investigations have been criticised as undermining state police autonomy — a federalism concern.

solution.concept_anchor: MLAT — CBI coordinates but MEA processes extradition formally
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students know CBI is the Interpol NCB and that MLAT is related to CBI's international work — the conflation of MLAT coordination with formal extradition requests is the precise trap the question exploits.
elimination_logic: Identify the correct attribute for each pair by recalling the distinction between MLAT coordination and formal extradition processing.
CBI as Interpol NCB is correct — CBI coordinates Red Notices and international intelligence. Eliminate pairs that misassign the NCB role.
Formal extradition requests are processed through MEA — not CBI. Any pair assigning extradition processing to CBI is incorrect.
FEOA 2018 allows CBI and ED to attach assets — not exclusive to ED. Eliminate pairs making it ED-only.
The correctly matched pair identifies CBI as Interpol NCB — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in option (b) switches CBI (Interpol NCB and MLAT coordinator) with MEA (formal extradition processor). Students who know CBI has international coordination functions may assign the extradition processing role to CBI, especially since extradition cases often involve CBI investigations. The distinction between coordination (CBI/MLAT) and formal diplomatic processing (MEA) is the precise knowledge gap exploited.
solution.final_explanation:
India's international criminal cooperation architecture distributes roles carefully across agencies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ministry of External Affairs, not CBI, is the formally designated authority for processing extradition requests. CBI's role is investigative coordination — not diplomatic extradition processing.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: This reverses CBI and MEA roles. CBI is the Interpol NCB and MLAT coordinator; MEA handles formal extradition. The pair incorrectly assigns formal extradition to CBI.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 empowers both CBI and ED to attach assets — not ED exclusively. This is a scope-extension error.
• Option (d) — Correct: CBI as India's National Central Bureau (NCB) for Interpol is accurate — CBI is the designated nodal point for all Interpol communications including Red Notices, diffusions, and bilateral criminal intelligence exchange.

Value Addition:
• CBI's Interpol NCB coordinates with foreign NCBs on fugitive tracking, evidence gathering, and asset tracing.
• Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) requests are coordinated through CBI for criminal matters — but the formal MLAT note is exchanged through diplomatic channels (MEA).
• India's extradition treaties prioritise specific bilateral treaties; where no treaty exists, the Extradition Act 1962 applies.

solution.concept_anchor: CBI suo motu power — Union Territory vs State distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the crime involves a central government employee — which students know places it within CBI's jurisdictional domain — without noticing that the location is a state, not a Union Territory.
elimination_logic: The scenario places the crime in a state — not a Union Territory or central premises. Identify this as the critical geographic fact.
CBI's suo motu power is limited to Union Territories and central premises. A state location requires Section 6 consent.
The state in the scenario has not given consent and CBI has no court order. CBI cannot register an FIR suo motu here.
The legally correct position is that CBI must first obtain state consent or a court direction — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap works by making the central government employee angle so salient that students overlook the state-territory location. A well-prepared student knows CBI covers central employees — and stops there. A precisely prepared student knows that even for central employees, if the crime occurs in state territory (not on central premises), the Section 6 consent requirement still applies unless there is a court order. The distinction between 'central employee' and 'central premises' is the fine geographic distinction exploited.
solution.final_explanation:
The scope of CBI's suo motu powers requires precise geographic and functional classification.

Applicable Principle: CBI's suo motu investigative power is geographically limited. It applies in Union Territories and in cases involving central government employees on central premises. When a crime occurs in state territory — even if the accused is a central government employee — CBI must obtain state consent (Section 6) or a court order before registering an FIR and investigating.

Scenario Analysis: The crime occurs in state territory. The state has not given consent. There is no court order. The accused being a central employee does not automatically place the matter within CBI's suo motu power.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This conflates 'central government employee' with 'central premises/Union Territory.' The geographic location of the crime — state territory — triggers the Section 6 requirement regardless of the accused's employer.
• Option (b) — Correct: CBI must secure either state government consent (general or specific) or a court direction before proceeding. Without either, CBI has no legal basis to register an FIR in this state.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Informing the NIA does not give CBI jurisdiction. NIA's suo motu power applies to scheduled offences — a corruption case is not in NIA's schedule.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 3 notification defines what CBI can investigate — corruption is already notified. The problem is territorial jurisdiction (Section 6), not subject-matter jurisdiction (Section 3).

Value Addition:
• The 'central premises' qualifier is crucial: if the same officer had accepted the bribe inside a central government building, CBI could potentially act suo motu.
• Court-directed CBI investigations overcome the Section 6 barrier — High Courts (territorial) and Supreme Court (nationwide) are the judicial routes.
• NIA's suo motu power is specifically for scheduled terrorist and security offences — not applicable to PC Act corruption cases.

solution.concept_anchor: Lokpal Act Section 26 and CBI Director collegium appointment

statement_analysis.statement: Section 26 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 empowers the Lokpal to authorise the CBI to conduct preliminary inquiries into cases involving public servants and to receive progress reports from CBI on such cases.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 26 is the specific provision that creates the Lokpal-CBI referral mechanism — both the power to authorise inquiry and to receive progress reports are explicitly provided.

statement_analysis.statement: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 directly amended the DSPE Act to introduce the collegium-type appointment mechanism for the CBI Director.
statement_analysis.reason: The Lokpal Act created the policy impetus for reform, but the actual amendment to the DSPE Act (inserting the PM + LoP + CJI committee) was done through a separate DSPE Amendment Act in 2014 — not directly by the Lokpal Act itself.

statement_analysis.statement: Under current law, both the Lokpal and the Central Vigilance Commission have supervisory powers over CBI, but in respect of different categories of offences.
statement_analysis.reason: Lokpal's oversight (under Section 26) relates to cases involving public servants referred by Lokpal; CVC's superintendence (under CVC Act) relates to PC Act offences — these are distinct but coexisting supervisory mechanisms.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is a strong distractor because the logical connection between the Lokpal Act (2013) and DSPE Amendment (2014) is so tight that students assume the Lokpal Act itself made the amendment, making Statement 2 feel correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Section 26 Lokpal — authorise preliminary inquiry + receive progress reports from CBI. Accurately describes the provision. Mark correct.

Statement 2: Claims Lokpal Act 'directly amended' DSPE Act — the amendment was made through a separate DSPE Amendment Act in 2014. Lokpal Act triggered but did not itself amend DSPE Act. Mark incorrect.
Statement 3: Both Lokpal and CVC supervise CBI but for different categories — this is correct. The coexistence of two oversight mechanisms with different scopes is accurate. Mark correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth: the Lokpal Act and DSPE Amendment are intimately connected — one created the political and legislative momentum for the other. However, they are legally separate instruments. The Lokpal Act does not contain the DSPE amendment itself; a separate amending act was needed. Students who know both reforms happened in close sequence may overlook the distinction between 'triggered' and 'directly amended.'
solution.final_explanation:
The Lokpal Act created a new layer of oversight for CBI while leaving CVC's existing superintendence intact.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 26 of the Lokpal Act is the operational link between Lokpal and CBI. Lokpal can authorise CBI to conduct preliminary inquiries into cases against public servants and mandates that CBI report progress back to Lokpal — creating accountability in the anti-corruption ecosystem.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Lokpal Act (2013) and the DSPE Amendment Act (2014) are two legally separate instruments. The Lokpal Act expressed legislative intent and the policy rationale; the actual modification to the DSPE Act's Section 4A (appointment of CBI Director by collegium) was enacted through a distinct amendment in 2014. Conflating the two instruments is a common but incorrect simplification.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Two oversight bodies now coexist: CVC (CVC Act, 2003) for PC Act corruption cases, and Lokpal (Lokpal Act Section 26) for cases involving public servants referred by Lokpal. These are complementary, not conflicting, oversight mechanisms.

Value Addition:
• The Lokpal itself is a statutory body constituted under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 — distinct from CVC which was constituted under the CVC Act, 2003.
• Cases not taken up by Lokpal can still be investigated by CVC/CBI through the standard PC Act mechanism.
• Section 26 creates a 'reporting back' obligation on CBI — adding transparency to Lokpal-referred investigations.

solution.concept_anchor: Police State List Entry 2 — basis of DSPE consent requirement
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both facts appear causally linked — students may reason that Entry 2 (police = state subject) directly explains why CBI needs state consent, accepting this as a complete causal chain without identifying that Entry 80 (Union List) actually validates the DSPE Act itself.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. 'Police' is Entry 2, List II (State List) — this places policing under state jurisdiction and is the constitutional reason why a central investigative agency cannot operate in states without consent.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. Entry 80 of List I covers extension of police powers of one state to another state — it does not directly validate Parliament's power to legislate on the DSPE Act. The DSPE Act's parliamentary validity actually flows from Entry 8 (Central Bureau of Intelligence and Investigation) of List I, not Entry 80.
Step 3: Moot — since R is factually incorrect, the answer is option (c).
A is correct, R is incorrect — correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This assertion-reason uses a reversed-causation technique in a subtle way: R contains an actual constitutional entry (Entry 80, List I) that does exist and does relate to police powers. However, Entry 80 covers extension of one state's police force's powers to another state — it is not the primary basis for Parliament's power to legislate the DSPE Act. The correct constitutional basis is Entry 8 of List I (Central Bureau of Intelligence and Investigation). A student who knows Entry 80 exists but not its precise scope will accept R as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional underpinning of CBI's federal jurisdiction requires distinguishing between multiple Seventh Schedule entries.

Assertion (A) Analysis: Correct. 'Police' is explicitly listed under Entry 2, List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule. This is the constitutional foundation for states' authority over policing and explains why a central agency cannot investigate in state territory without state consent — it would otherwise be trespassing on an exclusive state domain.

Reason (R) Analysis: Incorrect. Entry 80 of List I covers 'extension of powers and jurisdiction of members of a police force belonging to one State to any area outside that State' — this is about inter-state deployment of state police forces, not about Parliament's power to create a central investigative agency. Parliament's power to enact the DSPE Act derives from Entry 8 of List I, which covers 'Central Bureau of Intelligence and Investigation.' Entry 80 is frequently confused with this but serves a different purpose.

Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.

Value Addition:
• Entry 8, List I is the correct constitutional peg for the DSPE Act and CBI's parliamentary validity.
• Entry 80 is relevant when, for example, a state police officer is deployed in another state — a different constitutional scenario.
• Both Entry 2 (State) and Entry 8 (Union) operate simultaneously — states retain police power while Parliament creates a central investigative agency.

Reason (R): Parliament's power to enact the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, which governs CBI's operations, is drawn from Entry 80 of List I (Union List), which covers the extension of powers and jurisdiction of police forces across states.

statement_analysis.reason: CBI is under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions — not the Ministry of Home Affairs. This is a frequently tested distinction.

statement_analysis.reason: These three divisions accurately describe CBI's organisational structure — this statement is correct.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) '1 and 3 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 3 about the Director's rank is less commonly known, causing students who accept Statement 1 as correct (wrong ministry) to also question Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Ministry of Home Affairs — this is the entity-swap trap. CBI is under Ministry of Personnel. Mark as NOT correct.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 1 exploits the natural association between a law enforcement/investigation agency and the Ministry of Home Affairs. Students who know NIA, IB, and NATGRID fall under MHA naturally extend this to CBI. The Ministry of Personnel placement is counterintuitive — it reflects CBI's origins as a body primarily concerned with government employee corruption, not national security.
solution.final_explanation:
CBI's administrative placement and internal structure are both common sources of examination questions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (NOT correct): CBI falls under the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) within the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions — not the Ministry of Home Affairs. This distinction is one of the most exploited traps in UPSC questions on CBI.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CBI's three main divisions accurately reflect its operational mandate: Anti-Corruption Division (ACD) for PC Act cases, Special Crimes Division (SCD) for terrorism and organized crime, and Economic Offences Division (EOD) for bank fraud and financial crimes.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The CBI Director holds the rank equivalent to the Director General of Police — signifying the highest tier of the police hierarchy and ensuring the Director is not outranked by state DGPs in inter-agency situations.

Value Addition:
• The Banking Securities Fraud Cell (BSFC) sits within CBI's Economic Offences Division — a frequently tested sub-structure.
• CBI's placement under Ministry of Personnel reflects its historical mandate as an anti-corruption watchdog for government employees.
• The Prime Minister personally heads the Ministry of Personnel, making the PM the indirect administrative head of the CBI.

solution.concept_anchor: Landmark CBI cases — Vineet Narain Continuance Mandamus and Coal Scam Caged Parrot
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places Vineet Narain (1997) with the 'caged parrot' observation — confusing the two most famous CBI-related Supreme Court interventions, both involving political interference concerns.
elimination_logic: 'Continuance Mandamus' is specifically associated with Vineet Narain (1997) — the Hawala scandal case. Match A with 3.
'Caged parrot speaking in its master's voice' is from the Coal Scam case (2013). Match B with 1.
State of West Bengal v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights (2010) established High Court power to direct CBI despite withdrawn consent. Match C with 4.
Article 142 'complete justice' is the provision used in Supreme Court-directed CBI investigations across multiple cases. Match D with 2.
Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between 'Continuance Mandamus' (Vineet Narain 1997) and 'Caged Parrot' (Coal Scam 2013) is the central trap. Both cases involve Supreme Court supervision of CBI on political corruption. Students who merge these two landmark cases will swap A and B, reaching an incorrect combination. The distinction requires knowing not just that both cases involve CBI independence but the specific judicial innovation or observation each produced.
solution.final_explanation:
CBI's judicial history is defined by a small number of landmark Supreme Court interventions, each producing a distinct legal principle.

Correct Matches:
• A–3 (Vineet Narain → Continuance Mandamus): In the 1997 Hawala scandal case, the Supreme Court innovated 'Continuance Mandamus' — a continuous writ keeping judicial supervision alive throughout the investigation, not just resolving a point and closing the matter.
• B–1 (Coal Scam 2013 → 'Caged Parrot'): In 2013, the Supreme Court characterised CBI as a 'caged parrot' after discovering that CBI had shared its investigation status report with the Law Ministry and PMO — entities with political interest in the coal allocation case outcomes.
• C–4 (West Bengal CPDR 2010 → High Court overrides withdrawn consent): This 2010 case established the landmark principle that a constitutional court's (High Court's) power to direct CBI investigation cannot be neutralised by a state government's withdrawal of general consent.
• D–2 (Article 142 → Complete Justice for SC-directed investigation): Article 142 is the constitutional provision powering Supreme Court-directed nationwide CBI investigations — the 'complete justice' instrument used in Vineet Narain and subsequent cases.

Value Addition:
• 'Continuance Mandamus' is a UPSC-favourite concept — it means the court retains supervisory jurisdiction continuously, not just at the conclusion.
• The 'caged parrot' observation led to immediate directions prohibiting report sharing with political executive.
• West Bengal CPDR (2010) remains the authoritative precedent on court override of consent withdrawal.
